text: The corpus is heavily weighted to the recent past. Of the works that carry a usable date, 59.8% are dated to 2026 H1 alone. section: The whale, one document that is a third of the text
text:
The whale, one document that is a third of the text
Any statistic about volume of text has to reckon with one document. A single piece of legislation holds 25% of all extracted characters in the corpus, and the next-largest is a course playlist. This is why the Method page caps every per-document text statistic at the 95th-percentile character count (151,151 characters), because an uncapped average is a measure of the whale, not the field.

title: A model of verified judgment
text:
This is a formal sketch, not a finished result. It turns the essay’s central claim, that generation got cheap while verification stayed dear, into the smallest model that makes the ending a comparative static rather than a mood. The economics is the author’s to own and refine. The parameters are illustrative, and the propositions are stated as sketches a referee would still want to break.
The essay’s argument is one sentence long. Producing plausible research became nearly free, while confirming that a result is real stayed costly, so the scarce factor is verified judgment. That sentence has an equilibrium behind it. Below is the smallest version I can write down honestly.

title: A model of verified judgment
section: Setup, a market for plausible results
text:
Setup, a market for plausible results
A unit continuum of authors each submit one paper to a gatekeeper (a journal, a funder’s panel, a data editor). A paper has quality \(q \in \{H, L\}\). A high-quality paper is a real result. A low-quality paper is plausible but false, the paper-mill output that reads like research and is not.
Two costs sit on the author. Producing a genuinely high-quality result costs \(k\), the real work, including the author’s own checking. Generating a plausible submission costs \(g\), and the premise of the whole essay is that \(g\) has collapsed toward zero. The price of a competent-looking draft is now a few dollars of inference. The menu-pricing literature is where that premise is measured. Menu Pricing of Large Language Models documents how model providers price generation down a demand curve, which is the supply side of the flood. Verification did not fall the same way, and that asymmetry (\(g \to 0\) while \(k\) stays bounded away from zero) is the entire engine here.
A published paper returns private value \(V\) (a line on the CV, a grant, standing). A low-quality paper that is caught returns a penalty \(\varphi \ge 0\) (the desk reject, the retraction, the reputational mark). Normalize the outside option (do not submit) to zero.


Grounding in the corpus
Dirk Bergemann, Alessandro Bonatti, Alex Smolin · Menu Pricing of Large Language Models paper, 2026 · 20,135w
Susan Athey, Fiona Scott Morton · Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare (NBER WP 34444) paper, 2025 · 18,941w

title: A model of verified judgment
text:
Verification technology, the scarce input
The gatekeeper chooses an audit intensity \(a \in [0,1]\), applied per submission. Read \(a\) as the probability that a low-quality paper is caught. Take \(\pi(a) = a\) for cleanliness, and assume a true result never fails the audit (no false positives, a simplification I return to). Auditing costs
\[
c(a. \theta) = \theta \, \psi(a), \qquad \psi' > 0,\ \psi'' > 0,\ \psi(0)=0,
\]
per submission, with \(\psi\) increasing and convex, so deeper checking is disproportionately expensive. The scalar \(\theta > 0\) is the cost of verification technology, human referee hours at one extreme and cheap agentic reproduction (the “referee factory”) at the other. This is the binding input. Verified judgment is what the model is short of, and \(c(a;\theta)\) is its price.

title: A model of verified judgment
section: The author’s problem, when honesty is incentive-compatible
text:
The author’s problem, when honesty is incentive-compatible
Given the audit intensity \(a\) the author expects, compare the three payoffs below.
\[
\Pi_H = V - k, \qquad
\Pi_L = (1-a)\,V - a\,\varphi - g, \qquad
\Pi_\varnothing = 0.
\]
An author invests in quality (chooses \(H\) over \(L\)) exactly when \(\Pi_H \ge \Pi_L\).
\[
V - k \;\ge\; (1-a)V - a\varphi - g
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\,(V+\varphi) \;\ge\; K - g .
\]
Solving for the audit intensity that just sustains quality gives the threshold
\[
\boxed{\,a^{*} = \dfrac{k - g}{V + \varphi}\,}.
\]
Proposition 1 (the separating threshold). A separating equilibrium (every submitted paper is high quality) is sustained if and only if \(a \ge a^{*}\), and \[
\frac{\partial a^{*}}{\partial g} = -\frac{1}{V+\varphi} < 0 .
\]
Intuition. Generation cost used to do the gatekeeping for free. When \(g \ge k\), faking costs as much as doing the work, \(a^{*} \le 0\), and no audit is needed, the old world, where writing a convincing fake paper was itself most of the labor of writing a real one. As \(g \to 0\) the threshold rises to its residual floor \(k/(V+\varphi)\). The discipline that generation cost supplied for nothing must now be bought as audit. Cheap generation does not corrupt the pool by making authors dishonest. It corrupts the pool by removing the tax that kept dishonesty unprofitable.
Volume moves the same way. When \(a < a^{*}\), low quality pays, and because a plausible submission is now nearly free the mass of such submissions is bounded only by the number of would-be authors, not by their budgets. The pool does not merely tilt toward junk, it floods.

title: A model of verified judgment
section: The gatekeeper’s problem, and the branch
text:
The gatekeeper’s problem, and the branch
Sustaining trust is worth something. Let \(B > 0\) be the per-submission value to the gatekeeper of a pool readers can trust, over a pool they cannot, the difference between a literature people build on and one they discount to reputation. The gatekeeper sets \(a \ge a^{*}\) (pays for trust) when the audit it requires is cheaper than the trust it buys:
\[
\theta\,\psi(a^{*}) \;\le\; B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\theta \;\le\; \bar\theta \equiv \frac{B}{\psi(a^{*})} .
\]
This is the branch, and it is a comparative static on one parameter.
Proposition 2 (the ending is priced by audit cost, not capability). Hold model capability fixed. There is a threshold \(\bar\theta\) such that the gatekeeper selects the audit ending (\(a \ge a^{*}\), verification mandatory and rewarded) if and only if \(\theta \le \bar\theta\), and the flood ending (\(a < a^{*}\), the pool pools) otherwise. The selected ending turns on the cost of verification \(\theta\), not on how good the models are.
Intuition. The same capability jump that drove \(g \to 0\), feeding the flood, also drives \(\theta \to 0\), because agentic reproduction can re-run an analysis, chase a citation, or re-derive a proof at inference cost. So capability pushes both levers. It raises \(a^{*}\) (Proposition 1, more audit now required) and it lowers \(\theta\) (that audit now affordable). Which effect the institution acts on is the ending. The technology does not choose. The journal, the funder, and the data editor choose, by deciding whether machine verification is required and rewarded.

title: A model of verified judgment
section: The flood as a capacity constraint
text:
The flood as a capacity constraint
The flood ending has a sharper reading than “gatekeepers declined to audit.” Let realized audit be \[
a_{\text{real}} = \min\!\big(a,\. R/N\big),
\] where \(R\) is refereeing capacity and \(N\) the submission volume. With human referees \(R\) is fixed at throughput. As \(g \to 0\), \(N \to \infty\), so \(R/N \to 0\) and \(a_{\text{real}} \to 0\) even for a gatekeeper who wants to audit. At fixed human capacity the audit ending is not merely unchosen, it is infeasible. The referee factory (\(\theta \to 0\)) matters precisely because it unbinds \(R\) from human throughput, because machine audit lets capacity scale with submissions. So the two endings map cleanly onto one structural question, does audit capacity scale with the flood, or not. When it does not, trust does not vanish so much as relocate. Readers condition on author identity and institution instead of on the audit, because the audit has gone uninformative. That is the whitelist world the essay names.

title: A model of verified judgment
section: A hybrid where trust is priced in a certification market
text:
A hybrid where trust is priced in a certification market
There is a third region between the two endings. Suppose a private certifier offers audit at price \(p\) per paper while the journal lags at \(a < a^{*}\). High-quality authors buy certification to separate. Low-quality authors do not, because for them the expected value of inviting scrutiny is below \(p\). Costly certification then re-manufactures the separating equilibrium the journal failed to enforce, trust becomes a good with a price, sold outside the journal. Whether this substitutes for gatekeeping or corrodes it (a two-tier literature of certified and merely-published work) is a market-structure question, and the market structure around AI is where Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare (NBER WP 34444) locates the welfare stakes. The scarce factor of the essay’s title, trust, is, in this region, literally a priced input.

title: A model of verified judgment
text:
What would move the result

The value of trust \(B\). If readers do not actually discount a flooded pool, if citation counts keep rising regardless of quality, then \(\bar\theta\) collapses and no audit is adopted at any cost. The audit ending needs a community that punishes pooling.
The penalty \(\varphi\). Enforcement (retraction that bites, reputational memory) lowers \(a^{*}\) directly. Cheap audit and weak penalties are substitutes for sustaining honesty. The cheapest path to the audit ending may run through enforcement, not intensity.
The asymmetry \(k\) vs. \(g\). The whole model lives on \(k\) staying bounded while \(g \to 0\). If genuine verification also gets cheap, if \(k \to 0\) with \(g\), then \(a^{*} \to 0\) and the problem dissolves. The essay’s wager is that the checked, human-audited part of \(k\) is exactly what does not fall. That wager is the model’s load-bearing assumption, and its most testable one.
Whether audit is machine-verifiable and mandated. \(\theta\) is realized institutionally, not technologically. A reproduction agent that exists but is neither required nor rewarded leaves \(\theta\) high in practice.







Limitations, this is a sketch. Two types, one period, one gatekeeper, no false positives, \(\pi(a)=a\), and no dynamic reputation or gatekeeper competition. Volume enters informally. A full treatment would microfound \(N(g)\) and let \(R\) be chosen. The parameters are illustrative and nothing here is estimated, the comparative statics are meant to be read as directions, not magnitudes. The economics is mine to get wrong and to fix. Corrections are the point of publishing a draft rather than a proof.

title: Ending B · The flood
text:
This is one of two endings. It begins from the same premises as Ending A · The audit, and the two paragraphs below are identical in both. It diverges only on the gatekeepers’ choice. Here, they do not choose in time.
By the end of 2028 the two endings inherit the same board. Generating plausible economics is cheap and getting cheaper. Checking it is not, and the corpus shows the field’s first response was to build filters. Verification tooling is the largest single kind of AI-for-research tool in the collection, audited by hand, ahead of every other kind. Agents rewarded the projects that were versioned, tested, and documented, so software-engineering discipline arrived through the back door. The embargoed research frontier that held coverage down does not open by itself. Mirrors appear on authors’ own sites as embargoes lapse, but the index reflects them only when someone runs the fetch again. Talent equalized as execution costs fell. Access stratified as infrastructure decided who could do the work. The profession is at once the observer of cheap intelligence and the thing being treated by it.
One decision has not resolved. Whether the field’s gatekeepers (journals, funders, data editors) make machine verification mandatory and rewarded is not a fact about the models. It is an institutional choice, and it is the choice that sorts the next three years. The models keep improving in both endings. The difference is entirely whether verified judgment, the scarce factor, gets priced and rewarded before the flood of plausible machine text outruns the humans left to supervise it. What follows changes only that one variable.
In this ending the gatekeepers hesitate, or move too slowly, and the flood sets the terms.

title: Ending B · The flood
text:
2029, supply outruns the referees
Generating a plausible empirical paper is now nearly free, and the supply behaves accordingly. Submissions climb against a refereeing capacity that cannot climb with them, because refereeing is the expensive human step and there is no more of it. Desk rejection rises, submission fees rise, triage models are wheeled in, and the same adaptive congestion the field documented in firms gaming regulators now applies to authors gaming reviewer models. A plausible machine paper passes roughly as often as it fails, which is often enough to poison the pool.
Nobody quite decided this. There was no vote to lower standards. The standards simply did not scale, and the absence of a gate was itself the decision.
The arms race is not hypothetical. The corpus already holds its opening move. academic-humanizer is a tool whose entire job is to strip the tell-tale patterns that AI detectors and wary referees look for, a countermeasure to verification, shipped as a free skill. In the flood, tools like it proliferate faster than the filters, because evading a check is cheaper than passing one honestly.


The countermeasure
academic-humanizer: Strip AI-Writing Tells from Papers and Grant Proposals tool, 2026 · 1,123w
Robert Novy-Marx, Mihail Velikov · Artificial Intelligence–Powered (Finance) Scholarship (JEL) paper, 2026 · 11,978w

title: Ending B · The flood
text:
2030, trust retreats to the whitelist
When public evaluation cannot keep up, trust retreats to what is cheap to check, reputation and network. By 2030 the working filter is a whitelist, read the people and groups you already trust, discount the rest unread. Insiders win, because the whitelist is the insider list. The open, credential-blind evaluation that the credibility revolution, economics’ decades-long turn to rigorous, evidence-first causal inference, spent a generation building erodes from the top down.
Underneath sits the reflexive version of the collapse the corpus warned about. The grunt work, the RA and predoc coding and cleaning that used to produce econometric judgment as a byproduct, is exactly what agents now do, so the apprenticeship that made verifiers thins out at the moment verification becomes the scarce input. The few who can still supervise a machine end-to-end are worth a great deal, and industry pays it, so the would-be verifiers are bought out of the academy. Fewer checkers, more to check.

Verified judgment stayed scarce and never got priced inside the academy, so it was priced outside it. The flood is what cheap intelligence looks like when trust is left unpaid.

title: Ending B · The flood
section: 2031, bifurcation, and the one thing that slows it
text:
2031, bifurcation, and the one thing that slows it
By 2031 the literature is trusted less than it was in 2020, and the field has split rather than failed. A small, whitelisted core stays reliable and legible. A large periphery of machine-assisted output is unread and unrefereed, present in the counts and absent from the conversation. The measurement upside the field was promised, whole new data categories, cheap corpus construction, is real but stranded, because a result nobody can afford to verify is a result nobody can afford to use.
There is one thing that slows the collapse, and the corpus kept naming it. Keep an audited ground-truth check somewhere in the chain. Where a human-labeled gold set sits between the machine and the claim, the work stays trustworthy regardless of how it was produced. That discipline does not need a journal mandate. An individual can adopt it, and the ones who do are the periphery’s only bridge back to the core. It is the escape route from Ending A, practiced privately because it was never made a rule.

title: Ending B · The flood
section: What would have to be true by 2030 for this to be the ending unfolding
text:
What would have to be true by 2030 for this to be the ending unfolding


A named journal or data editor publicly reports a refereeing-capacity crisis, a surge in submissions or desk rejections attributed to machine-generated manuscripts, without a working reproduction gate in place to absorb it.
The predoc and RA layer visibly shrinks or converts to data-operations roles, so the pipeline that produced human verifiers is measurably thinner.
Reputation and network gating displaces open evaluation, whitelists, invitation-only venues, and trust-by-affiliation become the practical way results are filtered.


If instead the gate closed before the referees broke, you are in Ending A · The audit.

title: Ending A · The audit
text:
This is one of two endings. It begins from the same premises as Ending B · The flood, and the two paragraphs below are identical in both. It diverges only on the gatekeepers’ choice. Here, they choose to reward verification.
By the end of 2028 the two endings inherit the same board. Generating plausible economics is cheap and getting cheaper. Checking it is not, and the corpus shows the field’s first response was to build filters. Verification tooling is the largest single kind of AI-for-research tool in the collection, audited by hand, ahead of every other kind. Agents rewarded the projects that were versioned, tested, and documented, so software-engineering discipline arrived through the back door. The embargoed research frontier that held coverage down does not open by itself. Mirrors appear on authors’ own sites as embargoes lapse, but the index reflects them only when someone runs the fetch again. Talent equalized as execution costs fell. Access stratified as infrastructure decided who could do the work. The profession is at once the observer of cheap intelligence and the thing being treated by it.
One decision has not resolved. Whether the field’s gatekeepers (journals, funders, data editors) make machine verification mandatory and rewarded is not a fact about the models. It is an institutional choice, and it is the choice that sorts the next three years. The models keep improving in both endings. The difference is entirely whether verified judgment, the scarce factor, gets priced and rewarded before the flood of plausible machine text outruns the humans left to supervise it. What follows changes only that one variable.
In this ending the gatekeepers say yes, and they say it early enough to matter.

title: Ending A · The audit
section: 2029, the gate closes, and it holds
text:
2029, the gate closes, and it holds
Agent-checked replication becomes a condition of publication, not a courtesy. The move starts where the infrastructure already existed, the data-editor function that had spent a decade making code-and-data availability a discipline-wide requirement, and it generalizes because the tooling to enforce it is now cheap. A submission arrives with its pipeline. The pipeline reruns from raw data to every table. A reproduction that fails is a desk reject. The reporting standard that got a name in 2026 is now the thing a methods section cites, the way a robustness section is cited, and the referee factory the field built for itself becomes the referee infrastructure the journals lean on.
The cost of producing a result keeps falling, so entry widens. A researcher without a large lab can run an agenda that would have needed one. Talent equalizes. This is the good news, and it is real.

title: Ending A · The audit
text:
2030, the unit of contribution moves
By 2030 the published literature is measurably more reliable than it was in 2020, for a plain reason. Every empirical claim that reaches print has survived an automated reproduction the 2020 literature never faced. The counterfeit-resistant objects gain value accordingly. A paper is easy to fabricate. A maintained dataset, a tested codebase, and a living document that reruns end-to-end are not, so the unit of contribution drifts toward them. Citation of record becomes a property of an object, a benchmark, a standard, a package, rather than of a single paper.
A market grows in the space the field had flagged as empty. Nobody had been modeling the market for verification itself, and now audit, certification, provenance, and liability for machine outputs become questions with funding attached. The assurance industry that regulation is conjuring hires economists to price model error and design certification markets. The escape route the corpus kept pointing at, keep an audited ground-truth check somewhere in the chain, is now the default architecture rather than a discipline of the careful few.

Verified judgment got priced. The scarce factor found a market, and the market paid for the checking the flood would otherwise have skipped.

title: Ending A · The audit
text:
2031, audit-first, and its cost
The audit layer is infrastructure by 2031, invisible the way preregistration became invisible. A cohort trained under audit-first pedagogy, graded on finding planted errors, examined orally on work that cannot be delegated, enters the field able to supervise machines it did not have to do the grunt work to understand, because the curriculum rebuilt the judgment the apprenticeship used to supply.
The honest cost sits underneath the good news. Talent equalized, but access stratified. The infrastructure that makes audit cheap, compute, restricted-data enclaves, maintained toolchains, is unevenly held, so the gap that widened is institutional rather than individual. The field is more reliable and less evenly staffed than it was, and both are consequences of the same choice.

title: Ending A · The audit
section: What would have to be true by 2030 for this to be the ending unfolding
text:
What would have to be true by 2030 for this to be the ending unfolding


At least one top-five journal or the AEA Data Editor runs mandatory agent-based reproduction on submissions, with a failed reproduction treated as grounds for rejection, as policy rather than pilot.
A maintained, cited reporting standard for machine-assisted measurement is in routine use, appearing in methods sections and backed by at least one maintained validation suite rather than a scatter of personal repos.
Hiring and teaching reward the audit skill, research-assistant and predoc postings ask for verification and replication competence, and audit-style assessment appears in graduate syllabi.


If instead refereeing capacity broke before the gate could close, you are in Ending B · The flood.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
text:
This is a map of one research field, economics meeting AI, built from a collection of 661 resources, 490 of them with their full text attached. It is organised around an observation the collection makes unavoidable: this field argues in several registers at once, papers and Substacks and tools and podcasts, and those registers move at different speeds, carry different knowledge, and barely cite each other. Understanding that structure explains more about the field than any single paper in it. The first half maps the structure and what produced it. The second forecasts the next two to five years, with numbered probabilities, and closes with where a person might actually stand.
The collection did not come from one search. A pipeline watches where this field publishes: journal sites and working-paper series, but also newsletters, personal websites, GitHub repositories, course pages, and recorded talks. It fetches full text wherever that can be legitimately obtained and files everything in one database, alongside material added by hand. Every number below about the past is recomputed from that database at build time. Nothing is typed from memory. Claims about the future are numbered from P1, 15 in all, each dated and carrying a probability. What this map cannot verify is stated on the Method page, which also documents a date-layer repair made on 2026-07-27 that moved several works between periods.
It is not the field. It is one curator’s map of the field, and like any map it shows the mapmaker’s routes as well as the territory.

The most authoritative register is the least readable. section: The registers barely cite each other
text:
The registers barely cite each other
Registers would be a curiosity if they were just packaging. They are not, because the collection also records what every document links to. Restricting to links that land on something else in the collection gives a rough map of who points at whom.








Figure 1





Each register is largely talking to itself. 56% of a paper’s in-corpus links land on another paper. 58% of a tool’s land on another tool. Guides point at guides and at tools. This is what a set of parallel conversations looks like, and it is the single most useful thing on this page.
The interesting part is the asymmetry. Commentary and Substack writing point up at the formal literature: 52% of what an essay links to is a paper. The formal literature does not point back. Only 4% of a paper’s links reach a guide. So method knowledge flows into the informal layer, gets refined there, and has no return path into the citation economy. A researcher can produce the most useful methodological artifact of the year, and the mechanism that converts contribution into credit will not see it.
That asymmetry is the field’s central inefficiency, and most of what follows, including where the opportunities are, is downstream of it.
One channel is opening. 19% of what papers link to is now a tool, which is papers beginning to cite software as infrastructure they depend on. Software is the first informal artifact acquiring a citation path. If a reporting standard or a validation package becomes citable the same way, the loop closes. Whether it does is the substance of the forecast below.

Of the 8 people who write in three or more registers, 6 are also among the 10 most-credited people in the whole collection. The bridge is not a separate population from the establishment. It is the establishment, writing in a second register.
That inverts the obvious reading. The informal layer looks like an open frontier where anyone can build a reputation, and it is, but the people supplying it are overwhelmingly the ones who no longer need it. Writing where no credit accrues is cheap if you already have tenure and expensive if you are counting publications. So the bridge has a seniority gate that nobody placed there deliberately, and “just write in a second register” is advice whose cost falls almost entirely on the people least able to pay it. What the registers are made of
Knowing how the registers connect is one thing. Looking at what is actually inside them turns up two more splits, and both matter more than the format story on its own.
The literature studies one company’s product; the profession runs on another’s. Counting which model vendor each document’s own text talks about: among papers, the OpenAI stack leads 80 documents to 50 out of 141 with full text. Among guides it inverts, 30 to 23 out of 43, and 23 of the 129 guides and tools name the Anthropic stack without mentioning OpenAI at all. ChatGPT is what the field studies, because it is what the public adopted and what the usage data covers. Claude is what the field works in, because that is where the agentic tooling landed first.
The consequence is a dependency nobody in this collection writes about. The entire codified method layer, the instruction files and skills and workflow guides that Part 2 shows carrying the field’s practical knowledge, is written against one company’s product surface. That knowledge is real, but a good share of it is denominated in a vendor’s interface conventions rather than in transferable technique, so it depreciates on that vendor’s release schedule rather than on the field’s. Set that beside Acemoglu’s own point later in this map, that open-weight commoditisation could leave the labs unprofitable even if the technology succeeds, and the exposure is obvious: the profession has invested heavily in tacit knowledge whose carrier is a commercial product line. section: 2023 to 2024 · the guide arrives before the literature
text:
2023 to 2024 · the guide arrives before the literature
The first durable artifact was not a finding. It was a manual. Anton Korinek’s Generative AI for Economic Research appeared in the Journal of Economic Literature in late 2023 and was then kept alive on its own site, updated on a cycle faster than journals move, because the tooling it described would not sit still. A journal article behaving like software is the whole structural story in one object: when producing advice got cheap, keeping it current stopped fitting the publication cycle.
The theory arrived alongside it. Daron Acemoglu’s The Simple Macroeconomics of AI in May 2024 put a number on the decade, and Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s Generative AI at Work found a real productivity gain in a customer-support centre, concentrated among the least experienced workers. That paper is also a good illustration of why this page counts works rather than rows: it circulated from 2023 and reached the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025, so the finding is older than its position on any timeline built from publication dates.
The tension that has never resolved was visible immediately. Micro gains looked real; firm-level gains kept failing to appear. Economists have seen this movie, and the explanations on offer, short-run losses before long-run gains, revenue that arrives late, missing organisational complements, are all one claim: the machine is cheap and the things that make it pay are not.

text:
2025 H2 · the split becomes visible
Two things happen at once, in different registers, and this is the moment the structure described in Part 1 sets.
In the formal register an agenda gets built. The NBER convenes a workshop on the economics of transformative AI and publishes a research agenda. Korinek follows his guide with AI Agents for Economic Research, the moment “agent” becomes a research word. Diane Coyle and John Poquiz argue in Making AI Count that measurement itself is the frontier. The first large-scale usage evidence lands with How People Use ChatGPT. And the direction-of-innovation question sharpens: Pascual Restrepo’s We Won’t Be Missed marks the point past which steering technology stops working and only redistribution is left.
In the informal register, almost entirely outside the journals, the actual methods start moving. Pedro Sant’Anna publishes his own working setup. Scott Cunningham works through agentic workflows in public on Substack. Claes Bäckman turns his learning curve into guides for PhD students. Aniket Panjwani teaches economists to run agents. Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham builds a figure from an empty folder in public, diffs and all.
Note what each register is carrying. The formal one is producing claims about the world. The informal one is producing knowledge about how to work. Almost none of the second kind carries a date, which is why it is nearly invisible in the chart above and why it took a link analysis rather than a timeline to see it at all.
These writers were not inventing the practice. They were translating it, from a software world that had been running agents against test suites for a year already, and the standing claim in this literature is that economics receives that practice six to eighteen months late. That figure is repeated across the informal register and it matches the shape of what is here, but it is folklore: nothing in this collection establishes it, and this page is not going to assert a number it has not measured. It can be measured, and the last section of Part 5 says how.

section: 2026 H1 · the record floods, and tooling becomes a register
text:
2026 H1 · the record floods, and tooling becomes a register
59.8% of every dated work in the collection falls in this one half-year. Part of that is real and part is an artifact of when the collection was assembled, because a collector always finds the recent past first. What is unambiguous is that tooling appears as a register for the first time: the collection holds 114 tools, and essentially none of them predate 2026.
The literature, in four movements. First, the productivity ledger stays unsettled, with the adoption gap itself becoming an object of study in Mind the Gap and the financial question posed directly as speculative growth or bubble. Second, the task arithmetic breaks down in both directions: Gans and Goldfarb’s O-Ring Automation shows that automating some tasks raises the value of the human work left, while a companion model of chaining tasks shows automating a whole sequence pays more than the sum of its steps. The exposure scores themselves turn out to be unstable under re-measurement, and the counterweight is genuinely new work, whose appearance is a policy choice, which is what Acemoglu, Autor and Johnson mean by building pro-worker AI.
Third, AI enters the papers twice over: as an actor that trades, splits an ultimatum-game pie in How Does AI Distribute the Pie?, gives advice that shifts with perceived gender, and appears as a general social agent; and as an instrument that builds a decades-long capital-controls dataset impractical by hand. Fourth, the dark line. Novy-Marx and Velikov demonstrate that models generate complete finance papers from templates, and Acemoglu, Kong and Ozdaglar’s knowledge collapse model shows better AI can leave society less knowledgeable once it substitutes for effortful learning.
And the field started studying itself. Verification became a category: reading the 114 tools one by one, 21 (18.4%) exist to check another machine’s output, which makes verification the largest single kind of tool the field builds. Treat that as a count, not a share: the share moves with what the collection happens to hold, the count moves with the field.
Look at what those verifiers check, though, and the referee factory turns out to be building the cheap half. Of the 21 verification tools, 17 check a manuscript — referee reports, citation checkers, an AI-text detector — and only 3 check a result, by re-running an analysis, scoring a replication, or benchmarking a model’s output. The field’s own epistemics, from the Ludwig–Mullainathan–Rambachan framework onward, say the scarce thing is validated measurement. The tooling is overwhelmingly aimed at prose. Reading a draft is cheap to automate; re-running someone’s analysis is not, and the tools went where the cost was low rather than where the risk is.
There is a second gap on top of that one, and it is the sharper of the two. None of these verifiers has itself been validated against human referees. The corpus holds exactly one controlled head-to-head anywhere near the question, Toda’s test of whether models can refute a false economic theory, and that is about theory rather than refereeing. So the field has built its filters and skipped the step it insists on for every other instrument: benchmark it against the humans it replaces, before trusting it. The auditors are unaudited, which is the thesis of this page turned on its own favourite artifact. P14 bets on the first gap closing.
The cast overlap sharpens too. Gans authors both the formal model of jagged intelligence and the essay on vibe researching; Goldsmith-Pinkham co-authors the radiology complementarity paper and writes Research in the Time of AI. Economics is simultaneously the observer and the treated unit.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
section: 2026 H2 · the podcast becomes a register of record
text:
2026 H2 · the podcast becomes a register of record
The most recent material in the collection is not a paper. It is two long interviews, given weeks apart in July 2026 by the two economists whose names appear most often in everything above. They disagree about nearly everything except the one thing that matters here, and the fact that this exchange happened in podcasts rather than in print is itself the argument of Part 1.
Daron Acemoglu returns to his own 2024 number and largely keeps it: roughly 1.5% of GDP over ten years, and he still defends the order of magnitude. What he concedes he got wrong is speed in one place, agentic AI arrived faster and more convexly than he predicted, and 2026 is the first year that could change the diffusion path, because agents make the tools usable by firms that could never have integrated them. What he does not concede is capability: the models lack judgment, context, and any physical capacity, so claims that AI could already do most of the work in a field like finance are exaggerated, and acting on them would create a mess humans must clean up. His verdict on the current path is specific. Asked whether the productivity gain arrives as more output or as less employment, he answers “definitely less employment,” because the agenda being funded is an automation agenda rather than a pro-worker one, and that is a choice rather than a property of the technology. He is equally direct on the financial structure, contrasting the durable fibre of the dot-com boom with GPUs whose useful life is a year or two, and noting that commoditisation by open-weight competitors could leave the labs unprofitable even if the technology succeeds completely.
Erik Brynjolfsson takes the opposite side and says so, calling AI under-hyped and reporting that he is winning a wager with Robert Gordon that 2030 productivity will beat official forecasts. His evidence is sharper than his optimism. The Stanford “canaries in the coal mine” work finds employment for under-25s in the most exposed occupations down about 16%, with the effect growing monthly, while the least-exposed occupations and older workers grow. The mechanism he offers is elasticity rather than exposure: where demand is elastic, making a task cheaper raises spending on it, which is why there are more radiologists than ever despite the imaging being automated; where demand is inelastic, the same efficiency destroys the job. He is blunt about the institutional failure this implies. Removing the base of the career pyramid is individually rational for each firm and collectively ruinous, “a coordination problem,” because the junior roles were how senior judgment got made. And he draws the free-trade parallel deliberately: economists won the efficiency argument, never delivered the compensation, and got a backlash.
Both men, arriving from opposite directions, land on the same residual. Acemoglu: the models are useful but “you still have to verify and check certain things that they do.” Brynjolfsson: a project is defining the question, executing it, and evaluating the result; agents are taking the middle one, so the human job becomes the first and the third. Two people who agree on almost nothing agree on where the value settles.
The rest of the half-year fills in around them. Sixteen Nobel laureates and a group of leading economists and AI researchers published a “We Must Act Now” statement on preparing for AI’s economic transformation. Matthew Jackson and Zafer Kanik put benefits, costs and inequality policy in one framework. And the practice literature kept compounding, with Goldsmith-Pinkham on integration and collaboration and Bäckman shipping his referee skills as installable software, which is the informal register turning into the tooling register in a single step.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
section: One sentence, and why the structure follows from it
text:
One sentence, and why the structure follows from it
Intelligence became cheap and trust did not, so the new scarce factor is verified judgment. When a judgment task, classifying, screening, advising, drafting, refereeing, becomes almost free, its old price turns out to have been quietly paying for quality control. Once the task costs nothing, the value and the risk migrate to whoever still checks the work.
The register structure is what that looks like institutionally. Execution knowledge, how to actually get a machine to do the work, depreciates in months, so it settled in the fast, undated, open registers. Claims about the world need to be defensible for years, so they stayed in the slow, dated, gated one. The reason the two barely cite each other is not snobbery. It is that the credit system was built for durable claims and has no mechanism for perishable know-how. Every recommendation in Part 4 is an attempt to arbitrage that gap.

Producing a result got cheap. Trusting one did not. Every institution in this field is now reorganising around that single price change, and the register structure is the first visible consequence.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
text:
Where the evidence argues back
Three objections are strong enough to state properly, and the collection supplies both the challenge and the reply.
The bottleneck is taste, not checking. Ning Li’s Ideation Bottleneck decomposes the quality gap between AI-generated and human research and attributes the large majority of it, roughly 71% on its own numbers, to idea quality rather than execution. If ideation binds, verification is not the scarce factor. The reply concedes ground and holds the line: you cannot make a rule that people have good taste, but you can make a rule that work gets checked, so institutions organise around the thing they can enforce. Brynjolfsson effectively splits the difference by putting the human residual in both asking the question and evaluating the answer.
Trust got cheap too. Alejandro Lopez-Lira’s ZeroPaper generates a full research paper for about two dollars; Coarse, an AI referee, returns a report for under two. If checking is as cheap as producing, verification is not scarce either. The reply is that a cheap check moves the problem up a level: who checks the checker? The scarce thing is not the filter but the anchor it rests on, a human-labelled benchmark, a pipeline that reruns, a check somebody stands behind. Alexis Akira Toda ran the controlled test: no model refuted a false economic theory unguided, and human-plus-machine beat both the unaided machine and, in that setting, peer review.
The map is the mapmaker’s. This collection leans toward methods and tooling, partly because the curator studies his own trade. It also carries a development-economics thread the thesis never touches, including a living evidence bank on AI in development, and that thread widens the claim: where labour is scarce, full automation can help more, and the scarce-trust story shares the stage with a scarce-labour one. Disclosed, not hidden.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
section: Four positions, and what each costs
text:
Four positions, and what each costs
The translator. Be one of the 27. Write in more than one register about the same work: the paper and the guide, the result and the repo. The measurement says under one credited person in ten does this, which is why the ones who do are disproportionately cited. The cost is real, a second register is a second body of work with its own conventions, and the informal half earns attention rather than formal credit. It pays when attention converts, into invitations, collaborations, students, and consulting.
State the catch plainly, because the data does: 6 of the 8 deepest bridge-crossers are also among the 10 most-credited people here. This is a position the credit-secure occupy cheaply and the credit-insecure occupy at real risk. If you are pre-tenure, the honest version of this advice is not “write more guides.” It is: pick one artifact, make it citable (see the next position), and let it do the work of both registers at once.
The instrument-builder. Papers now send 19% of their in-corpus links to tools, the one channel where an informal artifact is acquiring a citation path. Building the thing others measure with, a validation package, a benchmark, a labelled gold set, buys a durable position because whoever hosts the benchmark quietly referees the field. The cost is maintenance, which is the quiet killer of research software, and the discipline required is unglamorous: version it, test it, document it, and expect to still be answering issues in three years.
The verifier. Verification is already the largest single kind of tool the field builds, and the 2026 evidence is consistent that perceived helpfulness is not audited correctness, in radiology, in healthcare delivery, and in coding audits. The unclaimed ground is not another AI referee, of which there are many, but the anchor underneath: the human-labelled ground truth a machine check rests on, and the economics of the audit market itself, liability for model error, certification design when auditors use the same models as the audited. That literature barely exists, and regulation is conjuring demand for it.
The measured version of that opening is sharper than the argument for it. Only 3 of 21 verification tools check a result rather than a manuscript, and not one of the 21 has been benchmarked against human referees. Two concrete, unclaimed projects follow directly, and both are small enough for one person: benchmark the referees — run the existing AI reviewers against a set of papers with known referee outcomes and publish the agreement statistics — and build the results-checker the field skipped. The first is a paper economists are unusually well equipped to write, because inter-rater agreement and error propagation are solved furniture in this discipline and novel in AI evaluation. It is also the single clearest instance of the export opportunity: a method economics already owns, aimed at a problem the AI field has not solved.
The domain holder. The generic “AI and labour” space is crowded and commoditising. What does not commoditise is privileged access: a firm register, an administrative dataset, a language, a regional network. Adoption gaps across countries are now a measured object of study, and someone with a good national registry is holding the scarce input for exactly that question. The cost is that access is institutional, slow, and non-portable, which is also precisely why it is defensible.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
text:
Practical rules the evidence supports

Read down, publish up. Take method from the fast registers, guides, repos, threads, because that is where current practice actually lives and it is 96% readable. Put claims in the slow register, because that is still where credit is conferred. Do not confuse the two directions.
Treat the podcast as literature. A talk in this field transcribes to roughly 10,090 words, and senior people say things there they will not put in print, as the Acemoglu and Brynjolfsson interviews show. Skipping them because they are not typeset is a real information loss.
Build the audit habit before you need it. Redo a machine-produced result by hand from time to time and log your own error rate. This is the individual version of the whole thesis, it needs no journal mandate, and the persistence evidence says the skill erodes precisely when you stop practising it.
Version everything, because the agent makes you. Agents work well only in projects that are versioned, tested and documented, so adopting them smuggles software-engineering discipline in through the back door. A decade of open-science exhortation achieved less than the tool did.
Prefer counts to shares whenever you control the denominator. This page had to correct its own headline statistic on exactly this ground, which is documented on the Method page.
Do not let your method knowledge be denominated in one vendor. 23 of 129 guides and tools here name one company’s stack and no other. Write down the technique — the gold set, the agreement statistic, the rerunnable pipeline — separately from the product that currently implements it, because the technique is what survives a release note.
Check before you forecast. The set of predictions on this page lost four claims that turned out to be true already, one of them by eighteen months. Checking cost an afternoon.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
section: What this map still cannot measure
text:
What this map still cannot measure
One number in this document is inherited rather than measured, and it should be named as such. The claim that practice knowledge reaches economics six to eighteen months after the software world is folklore: it is repeated across the informal register, it matches the shape of what is here, and nothing in this collection establishes it. It violates the rule the rest of the page runs on.
It is also measurable with what is already in the database, which is the interesting part. The corpus holds dated documents across every register and a full-text search index over all of them, so the first appearance of a term — agent, skill, instruction file, MCP, evaluation harness — can be dated per register. The gap between a concept’s first appearance in a thread or guide and its first appearance in a working paper is the diffusion lag, measured per concept rather than asserted once. Two version pairs already visible here suggest the lag is longer than the folklore says: Generative AI at Work circulated from 2023 and reached the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025, and “agent” moved from the practice guides of early 2025 to a titled NBER working paper in September 2025.
That table is the most obviously missing chart on this site, and it is the next thing to build. Until it exists, treat “six to eighteen months” as the placeholder it is.

title: How Economics Absorbed AI
text:
If you are early-career
The structural news is bad and specific, and it comes from the two interviews rather than from any paper: entry-level roles in the most exposed occupations are shrinking, and the junior rung was how senior judgment used to get made. Brynjolfsson calls the result a coordination problem, individually rational for each employer and collectively ruinous. Expect nobody to solve that for you soon.
What follows from the structure is that the substitutable skill is execution, which is exactly what agents took, and the scarce ones are the two ends Brynjolfsson names, asking the right question and evaluating the answer. Acemoglu’s version is the same residual from the other side: the models lack judgment and context, so those remain yours to supply. Concretely, that argues for building verification competence early rather than production speed, for owning a dataset or an instrument rather than a technique, and for being legible in a second register while the bridge is still only 27 people wide.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text: This document has two kinds of claim and no third kind. Claims about the past are recomputed from a database. Claims about the future carry a probability. This page describes the machinery behind the first kind and states plainly what it cannot support.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The data seam
One script, scenario/R/build_metrics.R, reads data/aiecon.sqlite (SELECT-only, it never writes the database) and emits tidy CSVs into scenario/data/derived/. The .qmd pages read only those CSVs, never the database. Renders stay fast, continuous integration needs no database logic, and a CSV diff makes every data change visible in git. Every number in the prose resolves to one of these files through the accessors in scenario/R/fig_helpers.R. None is typed by hand. The evidence blocks under each retrospective section are rendered from citations.csv, so the cited titles come from the database rather than from a writer’s memory. ev() fails loudly if a cited id is not in the corpus, which makes a fabricated citation impossible to ship silently.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The census, reconciled
This snapshot is pinned. The tree is Dropbox-synced and the corpus grows underneath it, so a document that claims “every figure recomputed, none asserted” cannot have its figures move with a sync. build_metrics.R is frozen to a fixed id manifest (scenario/data/snapshot_ids.txt), and re-pinning is a deliberate release step with its own script (scenario/R/repin_snapshot.R) that prints the old and new census side by side. This release re-pinned on 2026-07-27, from 385 resources to 661; nothing was dropped, because the corpus is append-only.
The mapping runs 661 indexed resources → 2 exact url_norm duplicates folded → title-dedup → 625 distinct works, of which 490 carry extracted full text. Earlier audits of this same corpus reported smaller censuses (294, then 385) because the corpus was smaller then. Those numbers are superseded, not contradicted. The AEA-2026 webcast page hosts two distinct talks (Li on the labour market, Ash on language models) sharing one URL. Those are kept as two works, not folded, because a shared landing page is not a shared work.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The flagship number, audited
The essay’s most quotable statistic, how much of the AI-research tooling is verification, was first produced by a keyword classifier (review|referee|replicat|reproduc|citation|audit|verif|integrity, frozen as VERIF_RE, and matched against titles only, because a resource’s description is curator’s notes that never enter anything this site publishes). Held to the discipline the essay preaches, that classifier fails an audit. Hand-labelled against a gold set (scenario/data/tool_labels.csv, one row per tool with a verdict, a one-word kind and a note), the audited numbers appear below.

Against the gold labels the keyword classifier has precision 93.3% and recall 66.7%. It now matches titles only, because a resource’s description is curator’s notes and never enters anything this site publishes, and that constraint is what makes it fail: the 7 false negatives are verifiers whose names say nothing about what they do (coarse, GPTZero, Thesify, Refine.ink, an adversarial research loop, a model leaderboard, an idea-evaluation pipeline), while the 1 false positive is a systematic-review screening platform with “Review” in its title that screens literature for humans rather than checking a machine. Naming is not function. The audited share, 18.4%, is what the prose and prediction P1 use.
That the essay had to correct a number it asserted, twice now, is not an embarrassment to hide. It is the thesis running on the document itself, because an unaudited filter is just more cheap intelligence. The gold labels are a small public dataset shipped with the site (scenario/data/tool_labels.csv, one row per tool with a verdict, a one-word kind, and a note). Adjust them and the number moves, in the open.






Read the count, not the share, across releases



The verification share fell from a published 11-in-38 to 21-in-114 between releases. That is not the field building fewer referees. The count of verification tools roughly doubled; the tool denominator nearly tripled, because the automated watcher began sweeping in general-purpose AI infrastructure (foundation models, agent frameworks, OCR engines, data APIs) that is not economics-research tooling at all. The share is a fact about this collection’s composition. The count is a fact about the field. Compare counts across releases, not shares.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The whale is mislabelled
The single largest document, 25% of all extracted characters, is indexed as “National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act.” It is not that Act. Its bytes are House Report 116-617, the full committee report accompanying the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act, of which the AI Initiative Act is one division. So a third of the corpus’s raw text is a mostly off-topic legislative document under a too-flattering title. The word headline is reported three ways. It is 4,909,337 uncapped, 3,684,149 with the whale removed, and 3,295,248 with the whale and the 388,901-word course-playlist transcript removed. Every per-document text statistic on this site caps document weight at the 95th percentile (151,151 characters) so the whale cannot drive an average.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The four hygiene rules
1. The version graph. The same work shows up as a working paper, a journal version, a video, and a thread. resources_clean.csv dedupes by normalized title before counting works, which folds 36 duplicate versions and leaves 625 works from 661 rows. Coverage keeps all rows, because coverage measures the index, not the field.
2. The whale. One document, a piece of AI legislation, holds 25% of all extracted characters. Any text-volume statistic caps per-document weight at the 95th percentile of character counts (151,151 characters). The headline word count (4,909,337) is kept uncapped to match the project’s measured claims passport, while every per-document average uses the capped figure (3,106,969). An uncapped average measures the whale.
3. Canonical names. Author names are diacritic-stripped and case-folded before distinct people are counted, so “Bäckman” and “Backman” are one person.
4. Dates. 382 of 661 rows (58%) carry no usable date. Undated rows are excluded from every time series and reported as a visible residual on the Timeline page, never silently dropped. A large part of that residual is not a gap at all: a tool homepage, a course catalogue and a living personal guide have no publication date and never will, so the pipeline records them as not applicable rather than missing. The rest stay undated and stay counted. A further 8 rows are known only to a year; they carry a January day-filler and therefore sort into that year’s first half, which is a sorting convention and not a fact about when they appeared.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
The date repair (2026-07-27)
This site placed several works in the wrong half-year until 2026-07-27, and the failure is worth recording because it was invisible from the prose.
build_metrics.R read the resources table’s raw date column, which is whatever the upstream feed supplied. It never read pub_date, the pipeline’s own derived date, which normalises the upstream string and fills gaps from sources that encode a date: the arXiv identifier, a /YYYY/MM/ permalink, and NBER’s own abstract page. The database held the better answer the whole time and the site did not ask for it.
Underneath that sat two wrong facts and one silent failure. The feed dated NBER working paper 33344 (Ludwig, Mullainathan and Rambachan’s measurement framework) to 2025-12; the publisher says January 2025, an eleven-month error that moved the paper a full half-year on this timeline. It misdated w34202 by four months. NBER assigns working-paper numbers in issue order, and scripts/lib/dates.R checks that relation is monotone before it will estimate any date from a w-number; those two errors broke monotonicity, so the estimator switched itself off exactly as designed and 43 further NBER papers silently lost their dates.
The repair replaces estimation with measurement. scripts/24_nber_dates.R reads the issue date off each NBER paper’s own abstract page (the Highwire citation_publication_date meta tag, or the visible “Issue Date” block) into a tracked file, data/nber_dates.csv, that records the URL and the date it was read for every row. All 69 NBER papers in the corpus were read this way, none failed, and the resulting series has zero monotonicity violations across 68 steps, which confirms the two bad feed dates were the whole problem. Dated resources rose from 188 to 278, and every one of them is now an exact date from a named source rather than an estimate: the interpolation rule is still in the code as a fallback and currently produces nothing.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
section: The metrics strip, and its forecast band
text:
The metrics strip, and its forecast band
The strip is measured through 2026 H1. After that, panels 2-4 draw an illustrative forecast band, a widening envelope from the last measured point to a range at 2028 H2. The bands are not themselves scored predictions. They are a visual aid, and their endpoints are set by the direction of the numbered predictions:

Tool share trends down (capabilities become product defaults), the direction of P9.
Verification share of tools trends up (the referee factory keeps growing), P1, P11.
Coverage recovers (embargoes lapse), P10.

Panel 1 (cumulative works by category) shows no projection at all past the measured data, because projecting a per-category stack would be a guess dressed as a measurement.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
What this document cannot verify

Curation is not coverage of the field. A curated corpus measures the curator’s map as much as the territory. The 59.8% of dated works landing in 2026 H1 is partly the field flooding and partly the newest material being the easiest to find. Where the distinction changes a number, the retrospective says so.
The verification-tool count is a hand judgment, not a measurement. Every tool was labelled by reading it, against one test: does it check another machine’s output? That test has genuinely hard cases (a systematic-review screener, a meta-analysis extractor, a paper generator that contains a reviewer), and a different reader would draw two or three of them the other way. The gold file ships with the site so a disagreement can be settled by editing a row rather than by argument.
The undated residual is not random. It falls hardest on exactly the material this page argues moves fastest: living guides on personal sites, which are revised rather than published and so carry no date by nature. Every time series here therefore under-represents the informal layer, and no reweighting fixes that, because the missing dates do not exist.
The narrative substance is not in the database. The story beats, which papers say what, are drawn from a separate analysis (docs/ai_in_economics_discussion_notes.md) and grounded in corpus rows by title. The database supplies the counts and dates. It does not adjudicate the interpretation.
The forecast is extrapolation. Nothing past 2028 is measured, and the claims there depend on institutional choices rather than model capability. That is stated at the branch, and the error bars are meant to be read as wide.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
Publishability
This site is designed to be publishable, so it obeys the same line the corpus’s own report obeys: aggregates and bibliographic facts only, counts, titles, authors, dates, tags. It never publishes the curator’s descriptions or fetched body text. Titles appear because they are bibliographic facts. The underlying documents do not.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
Rebuilding
# refresh the numbers from the database, then render the site
Rscript scenario/R/build_metrics.R      # SQLite -> scenario/data/derived/*.csv
quarto render scenario                   # CSVs -> _site/
The CSVs are committed, so the site renders in continuous integration without the database (the database is gitignored). Refreshing the numbers needs the machine that holds the corpus. Rendering does not.






Every figure on this site is recomputed from data/aiecon.sqlite at build time, and none is asserted. If the prose and the database disagree, the database is right.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
Indexing policy
What gets into the corpus, stated once so the “curator’s map” caveat has teeth. In: any resource on AI and economics worth a record, papers, working papers, guides, tools, courses, talks, threads, from any source, added through the seed feed or the hand-curated overlay. Full text in wherever it can be legitimately obtained. Where it cannot, the gap is recorded row by row rather than hidden. Out: nothing on topic is excluded for being informal or un-refereed, a Substack guide and an NBER working paper are both records, but a resource that is a door (a landing page pointing at content it does not itself contain) is marked as such and licenses no claim about what lies behind it. Changelog: the corpus is append-only. The frozen snapshot for this release is scenario/data/snapshot_ids.txt, and later releases re-pin deliberately, never by accident.

title: How this was built, and what it cannot verify
text:
Colophon
This document practises the four rules it describes. Machine assistance: the prose was drafted and revised with AI coding agents. Every past claim resolves to a corpus row through ev(), which fails the build on a fabricated id, and every number is recomputed by build_metrics.R rather than typed. Verified how: the tool classification was hand-labelled against a frozen gold set and its keyword classifier audited against it (above). The reconciliation, dedup, and whale relabelling were checked against the database. Where the gold sets live: scenario/data/tool_labels.csv and the snapshot manifest ship with the repository, so a reader can recompute the headline numbers. Frozen at: this release pins to the snapshot manifest. The tagged commit hash belongs here, and the forecast prose freezes at the tag while the retrospective and the predictions scoreboard keep updating. Not yet done, and owned by the curator: an external adjudication panel for the scoreboard, a browsable copy of the database, and publishing the gold set as a standalone dataset.

title: The predictions scoreboard
text:
This is the scoreboard, and it is the only page that changes after the document is tagged v1.0. The forecast prose freezes at release. The retrospective charts keep extending themselves as the corpus grows, and this table gains a resolution (a date, a verdict, and an evidence link) as each claim comes due.
Every prediction obeys the same rules. It is dated. It is binary or numerically measurable. It carries a probability in steps of 0.05. It names how it will be scored, whether from public pages or from this database directly. There are no hedged verbs anywhere in the set, and a claim that cannot be marked true or false does not belong here.
There is now a fifth rule, added the hard way: a prediction must not already be true.

Four claims were retired before publication, because they had already happened

title: The predictions scoreboard
text:
How scoring works
The cheapest claims to grade are the ones this database answers by itself. When the corpus is rebuilt each quarter, build_metrics.R recomputes the numbers that three of these predictions turn on. Those three are the verification-tool share (P1), the Coding-with-AI entry share (P9), and the embargo-resolution rate (P10), so scoring them is a script run, not a judgment call. The rest resolve from public pages. These are journal and data-editor policies, editor reports, job postings, syllabi, and citation searches, each named in the scoring column of predictions.csv.

These probabilities are a first pass and are meant to be reviewed before the v1.0 freeze. Once tagged, they do not change, because a forecast you can revise after the fact is not a forecast. Freezing also pins the definitions. The hand labels in tool_labels.csv, the 2026 H1 baseline P9 measures against, the embargoed-id list P10 tracks, and the shared reporting-standard definition P4 and P11 both use are all fixed at the tag, so a prediction cannot be scored against a moved goalpost. The document is designed to be graded in 2028 and again in 2031, and being wrong on the record is the point of writing them down.
P1 was also rewritten on 2026-07-27, before any freeze, and the reason is instructive. It originally required the audited verification share to hold “at or above 25%”. That share fell to 18.4% at the re-pin, not because the field built fewer referees, but because the collection’s tool denominator nearly tripled as the automated watcher swept in general-purpose AI infrastructure. A prediction whose truth depends on how the index happens to be composed is not measuring the world, so P1 now scores on counts and rank instead, which the composition cannot move. The lesson generalizes: prefer a claim about a count or an ordering to a claim about a share, whenever the denominator is something you control.
